--- title: "Lesson 17: Bootstrap Hypothesis Testing" subtitle: "BSTA 551: Statistical Inference" author: "Jessica Minnier" title-slide-attributes: data-background-color: "#006a4e" date: "2026-03-02" format: revealjs: theme: "../simple_NW.scss" chalkboard: true scrollable: true slide-number: true show-slide-number: all width: 1955 height: 1100 footer: Lesson 17 - Bootstrap Hypothesis Testing html-math-method: mathjax highlight-style: atom-one execute: echo: true warning: false message: false --- # Lesson 17: Bootstrap Hypothesis Testing {background-color="#2c3e50"} ## Review: Where We Left Off **Lesson 16: Further Aspects of Hypothesis Testing; CI-Test Duality** - Statistical vs. clinical significance: always report effect sizes + CIs - **Duality Theorem:** $\theta_0 \in$ CI $\iff$ fail to reject $H_0: \theta = \theta_0$ - Inverting a test gives a general CI construction method - Equivalence and non-inferiority testing via TOST / one-sided bounds . . . **Today's Goals:** 1. Understand the conceptual framework for **bootstrap hypothesis testing** (C&H Ch. 8) 2. Implement the **one-sample bootstrap test** by resampling under $H_0$ 3. Implement the **two-sample bootstrap test** 4. Understand **permutation tests** as an exact alternative to parametric tests 5. Compare parametric, bootstrap, and permutation tests: when does each apply? 6. Apply these methods to real medical data scenarios ## Roadmap | Topic | Key Idea | Reference | |-------|----------|-----------| | Why bootstrap testing? | When parametric assumptions fail | C&H Ch. 8 | | One-sample bootstrap test | Resample after shifting to $H_0$ | C&H 8.1 | | The naive bootstrap (wrong) | Resampling without shifting gives invalid null | C&H 8.1 | | Bootstrap p-value | Fraction of bootstrap statistics exceeding observed | C&H 8.1 | | Bootstrap vs. t-test | Robustness for non-normal, small samples | C&H 8.1 | . . . ::: callout-note ## Why This Matters Parametric tests (z, t) require distributional assumptions that may not hold in practice. The bootstrap test provides a **distribution-free** alternative that is valid under much weaker conditions — essential for small samples, skewed outcomes, and novel test statistics in biomedical research. ::: # The Bootstrap Hypothesis Test Framework (C&H Ch. 8) {background-color="#3498db"} ## Bootstrap CI vs. Bootstrap Test: Different Goals We have used the bootstrap to **construct confidence intervals** (Lessons 9–10). Now we use it for **hypothesis testing**. The ideas are related but not identical. . . . | Bootstrap CI | Bootstrap Hypothesis Test | |-------------|--------------------------| | Resample from estimated distribution | Resample from distribution **under $H_0$** | | Goal: capture sampling variability of $\hat{\theta}$ | Goal: approximate null distribution of test statistic | | CI covers $\theta$ with $\approx 1-\alpha$ probability | Null distribution used to compute p-value | . . . ::: callout-important ## Core Principle (C&H 8.1) A bootstrap hypothesis test approximates the **null distribution** of the test statistic by resampling from a population that **satisfies $H_0$**. The p-value is the fraction of bootstrap statistics at least as extreme as the observed value. ::: ## The Bootstrap Test: General Algorithm **Setup:** Observe $x_1, \ldots, x_n$. Test $H_0: \theta = \theta_0$ vs. $H_a: \theta \neq \theta_0$. Let $T = T(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$ be a test statistic. . . . **Algorithm:** 1. Compute the observed test statistic $T_{\text{obs}} = T(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$ 2. **Shift the data** to satisfy $H_0$: define $x_i^* = x_i - \bar{x} + \theta_0$ (so the shifted sample has mean exactly $\theta_0$) 3. For $b = 1, \ldots, B$: - Draw a bootstrap sample $x_1^{*b}, \ldots, x_n^{*b}$ **with replacement** from $(x_1^*, \ldots, x_n^*)$ - Compute $T^{*b} = T(x_1^{*b}, \ldots, x_n^{*b})$ 4. Compute p-value: $$\hat{p} = \frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^B \mathbf{1}(|T^{*b}| \geq |T_{\text{obs}}|)$$ ## Why Shift the Data? The fundamental challenge: we observe data from the **true distribution** (with $\theta \neq \theta_0$ possibly), but we need to approximate the distribution of $T$ **under $H_0$**. . . . **Shifting:** By replacing $x_i$ with $x_i^* = x_i - \bar{x} + \theta_0$, we create a dataset that: - Has the **same shape and variability** as the original - Has **mean exactly equal to $\theta_0$** (satisfying $H_0: \mu = \theta_0$) . . . ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} set.seed(42) n_shift <- 20 x_obs_shift <- rexp(n_shift, rate = 0.2) # right-skewed; true mean = 5 theta_0 <- 4 # null hypothesis value x_shifted <- x_obs_shift - mean(x_obs_shift) + theta_0 # Shared x-axis range across both panels x_range <- range(c(x_obs_shift, x_shifted)) x_pad <- diff(x_range) * 0.07 x_lims <- x_range + c(-x_pad, x_pad) # Compute shared density y-range for annotation placement dens_orig <- density(x_obs_shift) dens_shift <- density(x_shifted) y_ann_dens <- max(dens_orig$y, dens_shift$y) * 0.88 p_orig <- ggplot(tibble(x = x_obs_shift), aes(x = x)) + geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 10, fill = "#3498db", color = "white", alpha = 0.6) + geom_density(color = "#3498db", linewidth = 1.4) + geom_vline(xintercept = mean(x_obs_shift), color = "#e74c3c", linewidth = 1.5) + annotate("text", x = mean(x_obs_shift) + 0.5, y = y_ann_dens, label = sprintf("bar(x) == %.1f", round(mean(x_obs_shift), 1)), parse = TRUE, color = "#e74c3c", size = 5.5) + coord_cartesian(xlim = x_lims) + labs(title = "Original Data", subtitle = bquote("Mean = " * .(round(mean(x_obs_shift), 1)) * " \u2260 " * theta[0] * " = " * .(theta_0) * " (not satisfying " * H[0] * ")"), x = "x", y = "Density") p_shift <- ggplot(tibble(x = x_shifted), aes(x = x)) + geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 10, fill = "#27ae60", color = "white", alpha = 0.6) + geom_density(color = "#27ae60", linewidth = 1.4) + geom_vline(xintercept = theta_0, color = "#e74c3c", linewidth = 1.5) + annotate("text", x = theta_0 + 0.5, y = y_ann_dens, label = sprintf("theta[0] == %.0f", theta_0), parse = TRUE, color = "#e74c3c", size = 5.5) + coord_cartesian(xlim = x_lims) + labs(title = expression("Shifted Data (mean = " * theta[0] * ")"), subtitle = bquote("Same shape & spread" * " \u2014 " * "mean moved to " * theta[0] * " = " * .(theta_0)), x = expression(x^"*"), y = "Density") p_orig + p_shift ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](17_BootstrapHypothesisTesting_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-1-1.png){width=1344} ::: ::: # One-Sample Bootstrap Test (C&H 8.1) {background-color="#e74c3c"} ## Full Implementation: One-Sample Bootstrap Test **Medical Context:** A hospital monitors C-reactive protein (CRP, mg/L) as an inflammation marker. The healthy adult population norm is mean CRP = 1.5 mg/L. We observe a small sample of post-surgical patients and test whether their mean CRP differs from this norm. $$H_0: \mu = 1.5 \quad \text{vs} \quad H_a: \mu \neq 1.5$$ ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} set.seed(551) n_crp <- 22 # Gamma(shape=2, rate=1): mean = 2, SD ≈ 1.41 — right-skewed, moderate elevation crp_data <- rgamma(n_crp, shape = 2, rate = 1) mu_0 <- 1.5 B <- 5000 # Observed test statistic (t-statistic) T_obs <- (mean(crp_data) - mu_0) / (sd(crp_data) / sqrt(n_crp)) # Shift data to satisfy H0 crp_shifted <- crp_data - mean(crp_data) + mu_0 # Bootstrap T_boot <- replicate(B, { boot_samp <- sample(crp_shifted, size = n_crp, replace = TRUE) (mean(boot_samp) - mu_0) / (sd(boot_samp) / sqrt(n_crp)) }) # Bootstrap p-value (two-sided) p_boot <- mean(abs(T_boot) >= abs(T_obs)) # Parametric t-test p-value p_param <- t.test(crp_data, mu = mu_0)$p.value cat("Sample mean CRP:", round(mean(crp_data), 3), "mg/L\n") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Sample mean CRP: 2.083 mg/L ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} cat("Sample SD: ", round(sd(crp_data), 3), "mg/L\n") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Sample SD: 1.588 mg/L ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} cat("Observed t-statistic:", round(T_obs, 4), "\n") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Observed t-statistic: 1.7238 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} cat("Bootstrap p-value: ", round(p_boot, 4), "\n") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Bootstrap p-value: 0.1174 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} cat("Parametric t-test p: ", round(p_param, 4), "\n") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Parametric t-test p: 0.0994 ``` ::: ::: ## Visualizing the Bootstrap Null Distribution ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} t_df <- n_crp - 1 t_grid <- seq(-6, 6, by = 0.05) p_boot_null <- ggplot(tibble(T = T_boot), aes(x = T)) + geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 60, fill = "#3498db", color = "white", alpha = 0.7) + geom_line(data = tibble(x = t_grid, y = dt(t_grid, df = t_df)), aes(x = x, y = y), color = "coral", linewidth = 1.3, linetype = "dashed") + geom_vline(xintercept = c(-abs(T_obs), abs(T_obs)), color = "#e74c3c", linewidth = 1.5) + annotate("rect", xmin = abs(T_obs), xmax = Inf, ymin = 0, ymax = Inf, fill = "#e74c3c", alpha = 0.15) + annotate("rect", xmin = -Inf, xmax = -abs(T_obs), ymin = 0, ymax = Inf, fill = "#e74c3c", alpha = 0.15) + annotate("text", x = 4.5, y = 0.32, label = sprintf("p[boot] == %.4f", p_boot), parse = TRUE, color = "#e74c3c", size = 5) + scale_color_manual(values = c("Bootstrap" = "#3498db", "t(n-1)" = "coral")) + labs( title = "Bootstrap Null Distribution vs. t Distribution", subtitle = "Blue histogram = bootstrap; dashed red = t(n-1).\nRed shading = p-value region.", x = "t-statistic", y = "Density" ) # Also show original data vs shifted p_data_compare <- bind_rows( tibble(x = crp_data, type = "Original data"), tibble(x = crp_shifted, type = "Shifted data (H0)") ) |> ggplot(aes(x = x, fill = type)) + geom_density(alpha = 0.5) + geom_vline(xintercept = mu_0, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1) + scale_fill_manual(values = c("Original data" = "#3498db", "Shifted data (H0)" = "#27ae60")) + labs(title = "Original vs. Shifted Data", subtitle = expression("Vertical line at " * mu[0] * " = 1.5 mg/L"), x = "CRP (mg/L)", y = "Density", fill = NULL) + theme(legend.position = "bottom") p_data_compare + p_boot_null ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](17_BootstrapHypothesisTesting_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-3-1.png){width=1344} ::: ::: ## When Does the Bootstrap Test Outperform the t-Test? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} # Compare rejection rates under H0 (alpha control) for normal vs skewed distributions sim_compare <- function(n, dist = "normal", B_inner = 999, reps = 500) { replicate(reps, { if (dist == "normal") { x <- rnorm(n, mean = 0) } else { x <- rexp(n, rate = 1) - 1 # centered exponential (mean=0, skewed) } # t-test p-value p_t <- t.test(x, mu = 0)$p.value # Bootstrap p-value x_sh <- x - mean(x) # shift to H0: mu = 0 T_ob <- (mean(x)) / (sd(x) / sqrt(n)) T_bs <- replicate(B_inner, { bs <- sample(x_sh, n, replace = TRUE) (mean(bs)) / (sd(bs) / sqrt(n)) }) p_bs <- mean(abs(T_bs) >= abs(T_ob)) c(p_t = p_t, p_bs = p_bs) }) |> t() |> as_tibble() |> summarise( alpha_t = mean(p_t < 0.05), alpha_bs = mean(p_bs < 0.05), .groups = "drop" ) |> mutate(n = n, dist = dist) } set.seed(42) grid <- expand_grid(n = c(10, 25, 50), dist = c("normal", "skewed")) res <- map2_dfr(grid$n, grid$dist, sim_compare) res |> pivot_longer(starts_with("alpha"), names_to = "method", values_to = "type1") |> mutate( method = recode(method, alpha_t = "t-test", alpha_bs = "Bootstrap test"), dist = recode(dist, normal = "Normal population", skewed = "Skewed population (Exp-1)") ) |> ggplot(aes(x = factor(n), y = type1, fill = method)) + geom_col(position = "dodge", alpha = 0.85) + geom_hline(yintercept = 0.05, linetype = "dashed", color = "black", linewidth = 1) + facet_wrap(~dist) + scale_fill_manual(values = c("t-test" = "steelblue", "Bootstrap test" = "#27ae60")) + scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 0.12)) + labs( title = expression("Type I Error Rate Under " * H[0] * " at " * alpha * " = 0.05"), subtitle = "Both methods well-calibrated for normal; bootstrap slightly better for small skewed samples", x = "Sample size (n)", y = "Empirical Type I error rate", fill = NULL ) + theme(legend.position = "bottom") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](17_BootstrapHypothesisTesting_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-4-1.png){width=1344} ::: ::: ## What Happens If You Don't Shift? (A Common Mistake) It is tempting to simply bootstrap from the **original** data and compare to $\theta_0$. Why is this wrong? . . . ::: callout-warning ## The Naive Bootstrap Test — Incorrect Resample from the original $x_1, \ldots, x_n$ and compute $\bar{x}^{*b}$. Compare the fraction of $\bar{x}^{*b}$ farther from $\bar{x}$ than $|\bar{x} - \theta_0|$. **Problem:** The bootstrap distribution is centered at $\bar{x}$, not at $\theta_0$. It approximates the sampling distribution of $\hat{\theta}$, **not** the null distribution. ::: . . . ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} set.seed(551) n_demo <- 22 x_demo <- rgamma(n_demo, shape = 2, rate = 1) # true mean ≈ 2 mu_demo <- 1.5 B_demo <- 4000 xbar_demo <- mean(x_demo) # WRONG: resample from original, compare distance from xbar T_naive <- replicate(B_demo, mean(sample(x_demo, n_demo, replace = TRUE))) p_naive <- mean(abs(T_naive - xbar_demo) >= abs(xbar_demo - mu_demo)) # CORRECT: shift then resample x_sh_demo <- x_demo - xbar_demo + mu_demo T_correct <- replicate(B_demo, { bs <- sample(x_sh_demo, n_demo, replace = TRUE) (mean(bs) - mu_demo) / (sd(bs) / sqrt(n_demo)) }) T_obs_demo <- (xbar_demo - mu_demo) / (sd(x_demo) / sqrt(n_demo)) p_correct <- mean(abs(T_correct) >= abs(T_obs_demo)) p_ttest_demo <- t.test(x_demo, mu = mu_demo)$p.value p_nv <- ggplot(tibble(T = T_naive), aes(x = T)) + geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 50, fill = "#e74c3c", color = "white", alpha = 0.8) + geom_vline(xintercept = xbar_demo, color = "black", linewidth = 1.2) + geom_vline(xintercept = mu_demo, color = "#3498db", linewidth = 1.2, linetype = "dashed") + annotate("text", x = xbar_demo + 0.05, y = 2.5, label = "bar(x)", parse = TRUE, size = 5, color = "black") + annotate("text", x = mu_demo - 0.05, y = 2.5, label = "mu[0]", parse = TRUE, size = 5, color = "#3498db", hjust = 1) + labs(title = expression(bold("WRONG") * ": Naive bootstrap"), subtitle = sprintf("Centered at x-bar, not theta0 \u2014 p = %.3f (not a valid null distribution)", p_naive), x = expression(bar(x)^"*"), y = "Density") p_cr <- ggplot(tibble(T = T_correct), aes(x = T)) + geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 50, fill = "#27ae60", color = "white", alpha = 0.8) + geom_vline(xintercept = c(-abs(T_obs_demo), abs(T_obs_demo)), color = "#e74c3c", linewidth = 1.2) + annotate("text", x = abs(T_obs_demo) + 0.15, y = 0.32, label = bquote(T[obs] == .(round(T_obs_demo, 2))), color = "#e74c3c", size = 4.5) + labs(title = expression(bold("CORRECT") * ": Bootstrap from shifted data"), subtitle = sprintf("Centered at theta0 \u2014 Bootstrap p = %.3f, t-test p = %.3f", p_correct, p_ttest_demo), x = "t-statistic", y = "Density") p_nv + p_cr ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](17_BootstrapHypothesisTesting_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-5-1.png){width=1344} ::: ::: # Choosing Between Methods: One-Sample Tests {background-color="#f39c12"} ## Decision Framework For a **one-sample** test $H_0: \mu = \mu_0$, which method should you use? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} library(DiagrammeR) grViz(" digraph test_choice { graph [rankdir=TB, bgcolor=transparent, fontsize=18] node [shape=box, style=filled, fontsize=14, fontname='Helvetica'] A [label='One-Sample Test\nH0: mu = mu0', fillcolor='#3498db', fontcolor=white, width=4] B [label='Normal population\nor large n (CLT)?', fillcolor='#f39c12', fontcolor=white, shape=diamond, width=3.5] C [label='One-sample t-test\n(Most powerful for normal data)', fillcolor='#27ae60', fontcolor=white, width=3.5] D [label='iid observations?', fillcolor='#f39c12', fontcolor=white, shape=diamond, width=3] E [label='Bootstrap Test\nShift to mu0, resample', fillcolor='#e74c3c', fontcolor=white, width=3.5] F [label='Non-iid structure present:\nConsider GEE, mixed models,\nor time series methods', fillcolor='#95a5a6', fontcolor=white, width=4] A -> B B -> C [label=' Yes', fontsize=13] B -> D [label=' No', fontsize=13] D -> E [label=' Yes', fontsize=13] D -> F [label=' No', fontsize=12] } ") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ## Assumptions Compared | Assumption | t-test | Bootstrap test | |-----------|--------|----------------| | Normal population (or large $n$) | Required | Not required | | iid observations | Required | Required | | Distribution-free validity | No | Approximately | | Works for any test statistic | No | **Yes** | | Computationally intensive | No | Moderate | . . . ::: callout-tip ## Key Message The **bootstrap test** is the most flexible choice for one-sample problems with non-normal, skewed data — it only requires iid sampling and makes no symmetry assumption. The **t-test** is optimal when normality holds. Permutation methods will be covered after two-sample inference. ::: ## Simulation Study: Comparing t-test and Bootstrap How well does each method control Type I error, and what is the power, across different population shapes? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} run_onesample_tests <- function(n = 20, delta = 0, dist = "normal", B_inner = 499) { x <- switch(dist, normal = rnorm(n, mean = delta), skewed = rexp(n, rate = 1) - 1 + delta, heavyt = rt(n, df = 3) + delta ) mu_0 <- 0 # 1. Parametric t-test p_t <- t.test(x, mu = mu_0)$p.value # 2. Bootstrap test (shift-resample) x_sh <- x - mean(x) + mu_0 T_ob <- (mean(x) - mu_0) / (sd(x) / sqrt(n)) T_bs <- replicate(B_inner, { bs <- sample(x_sh, n, replace = TRUE) (mean(bs) - mu_0) / (sd(bs) / sqrt(n)) }) p_b <- mean(abs(T_bs) >= abs(T_ob)) c(p_t = p_t, p_boot = p_b) } set.seed(99) sim_grid <- expand_grid( n = c(15, 40), delta = c(0, 0.6), dist = c("normal", "skewed", "heavyt") ) sim_res <- sim_grid |> rowwise() |> mutate( sims = list( replicate(500, run_onesample_tests(n = n, delta = delta, dist = dist, B_inner = 299)) |> t() |> as_tibble() ) ) |> unnest(sims) |> pivot_longer(starts_with("p_"), names_to = "method", values_to = "pval") |> group_by(n, delta, dist, method) |> summarise(rejection = mean(pval < 0.05), .groups = "drop") |> mutate( method = recode(method, p_t = "t-test", p_boot = "Bootstrap"), dist_lab = recode(dist, normal = "Normal", skewed = "Skewed (Exp-1)", heavyt = "Heavy-tailed (t3)"), quantity = ifelse(delta == 0, "Type I Error (H0 true, target = 5%)", "Power (Ha true, delta = 0.6)") ) ggplot(sim_res |> filter(n == 15), aes(x = method, y = rejection, fill = method)) + geom_col(alpha = 0.85, width = 0.5) + geom_hline(yintercept = 0.05, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.8) + facet_grid(quantity ~ dist_lab, scales = "free_y") + scale_fill_manual(values = c("t-test" = "steelblue", "Bootstrap" = "#e74c3c")) + scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.1))) + labs( title = "t-test vs. Bootstrap: Type I Error and Power (n = 15)", subtitle = "Bootstrap maintains better Type I error control for skewed/heavy-tailed data at small n", x = NULL, y = "Rejection rate", fill = NULL ) + theme(legend.position = "bottom", strip.text = element_text(size = 12), strip.text.y = element_text(size = 11), plot.margin = margin(5, 20, 5, 5)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](17_BootstrapHypothesisTesting_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-7-1.png){width=1344} ::: ::: ## Simulation: Larger Sample (n = 40) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} ggplot(sim_res |> filter(n == 40), aes(x = method, y = rejection, fill = method)) + geom_col(alpha = 0.85, width = 0.5) + geom_hline(yintercept = 0.05, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.8) + facet_grid(quantity ~ dist_lab, scales = "free_y") + scale_fill_manual(values = c("t-test" = "steelblue", "Bootstrap" = "#e74c3c")) + scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.1))) + labs( title = "t-test vs. Bootstrap: Type I Error and Power (n = 40)", subtitle = "By n = 40, both methods converge — CLT smooths out distributional differences", x = NULL, y = "Rejection rate", fill = NULL ) + theme(legend.position = "bottom", strip.text = element_text(size = 12), strip.text.y = element_text(size = 11), plot.margin = margin(5, 20, 5, 5)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](17_BootstrapHypothesisTesting_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-8-1.png){width=1344} ::: ::: ## Key Takeaways from Simulation - **Normal data:** Both methods control Type I error well at $n = 15$ and $n = 40$; t-test has slightly higher power (it's optimal here) . . . - **Skewed data, small $n$:** The t-test can be slightly anti-conservative (Type I error > 5%); the bootstrap test maintains better control . . . - **Heavy-tailed data ($t_3$):** Similar pattern — bootstrap is more robust for small samples . . . - **Large $n$:** Differences wash out — the CLT rescues the t-test regardless of population shape . . . ::: callout-note ## Practical Implication For small samples ($n < 30$) with non-normal data, the bootstrap test is preferable. For $n \geq 40$, the t-test is nearly equivalent in practice. ::: # Bootstrap Tests and the Duality with CIs {background-color="#16a085"} ## Bootstrap Tests and Bootstrap CIs: Are They Dual? In the parametric setting, confidence intervals and tests are **exactly dual**. For bootstrap methods this is only **approximate** — and only when the CI and test use the **same pivot**. ::: callout-important ## The Key Condition - **Percentile CI** resamples from the original data and uses $\bar{X}^*$ as the pivot - **Bootstrap test** resamples from the shifted data and uses some test statistic $T^*$ - If both use the **same pivot** (e.g., raw mean), duality is approximate with only boundary disagreements from Monte Carlo noise - If they use **different pivots** (e.g., percentile CI with raw mean vs. test with standardised $t$), they can disagree systematically over a wide range ::: ## Demonstrating: Same Pivot vs. Different Pivots ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} set.seed(42) # Right-skewed small sample: CRP values (mg/L) crp_small <- c(1.2, 1.5, 2.3, 1.8, 4.7, 3.1, 1.4, 6.2, 2.0, 1.6) n_s <- length(crp_small) B_s <- 9999 xbar_s <- mean(crp_small) # Percentile CI (pivot: raw mean from original data) boot_means <- replicate(B_s, mean(sample(crp_small, n_s, replace = TRUE))) ci_lo <- quantile(boot_means, 0.025) ci_hi <- quantile(boot_means, 0.975) mu0_grid <- seq(0.8, 4.8, by = 0.05) scan_results <- map_dfr(mu0_grid, function(mu0) { x_sh <- crp_small - xbar_s + mu0 in_ci <- mu0 >= ci_lo & mu0 <= ci_hi # Same pivot: raw mean difference (matches what percentile CI inverts) T_ob_raw <- xbar_s - mu0 T_bs_raw <- replicate(B_s, mean(sample(x_sh, n_s, replace = TRUE)) - mu0) p_raw <- mean(abs(T_bs_raw) >= abs(T_ob_raw)) # Different pivot: standardised t-statistic T_ob_t <- (xbar_s - mu0) / (sd(crp_small) / sqrt(n_s)) T_bs_t <- replicate(B_s, { bs <- sample(x_sh, n_s, replace = TRUE) (mean(bs) - mu0) / (sd(bs) / sqrt(n_s)) }) p_t <- mean(abs(T_bs_t) >= abs(T_ob_t)) tibble(mu0 = mu0, in_ci = in_ci, p_raw = p_raw, p_t = p_t, agree_raw = in_ci == (p_raw >= 0.05), agree_t = in_ci == (p_t >= 0.05)) }) make_panel <- function(data, p_col, agree_col, pivot_label) { ggplot(data, aes(x = mu0, y = .data[[p_col]])) + annotate("rect", xmin = ci_lo, xmax = ci_hi, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = "#16a085", alpha = 0.12) + geom_vline(xintercept = c(ci_lo, ci_hi), color = "#16a085", linewidth = 1.0, linetype = "dotted") + geom_hline(yintercept = 0.05, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray40") + geom_line(aes(color = .data[[agree_col]]), linewidth = 1.6) + geom_point(data = filter(data, !.data[[agree_col]]), aes(x = mu0, y = .data[[p_col]]), color = "#e74c3c", size = 3) + scale_color_manual(values = c("TRUE" = "#006a4e", "FALSE" = "#e74c3c"), labels = c("TRUE" = "Agree", "FALSE" = "Disagree")) + annotate("text", x = mean(c(ci_lo, ci_hi)), y = 0.88, label = sprintf("95%% CI [%.2f, %.2f]", ci_lo, ci_hi), color = "#16a085", size = 5) + labs(title = pivot_label, x = expression(mu[0]), y = "Bootstrap test p-value", color = NULL) + theme(legend.position = "bottom", plot.title = element_text(size = 15, lineheight = 1.2), axis.title = element_text(size = 14), axis.text = element_text(size = 13), legend.text = element_text(size = 13)) } p_raw_panel <- make_panel(scan_results, "p_raw", "agree_raw", "Same pivot: raw mean\n(percentile CI approx. dual to bootstrap test)") p_t_panel <- make_panel(scan_results, "p_t", "agree_t", "Different pivots: percentile CI (raw mean)\nvs. bootstrap test (standardised t)") p_raw_panel + p_t_panel + plot_annotation( title = "Bootstrap CI-Test Duality: Matching vs. Mismatched Pivots", subtitle = "Green region = 95% percentile CI. Red points = mu0 where CI and test give contradictory decisions.", theme = theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 17), plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 14)) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](17_BootstrapHypothesisTesting_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-9-1.png){width=1440} ::: ::: . . . ::: callout-warning ## Key Lesson **Left panel:** Using the same pivot (raw mean), disagreements are rare and only occur right at the CI boundary due to Monte Carlo variability — duality is approximately satisfied. **Right panel:** Using different pivots (percentile CI vs. standardised $t$-test), disagreements are systematic and spread over a range — this is a methodological mismatch, not boundary noise. ::: # Key Takeaways {background-color="#2c3e50"} ## Key Takeaways ::: callout-important ## Today's Main Points (C&H Chapter 8) 1. **Bootstrap hypothesis tests** approximate the null distribution by resampling from data **shifted to satisfy $H_0$** — this is fundamentally different from bootstrap CIs (which resample from the original data) 2. **The naive bootstrap is wrong:** resampling from the original data without shifting produces a distribution centered at $\bar{x}$, not at $\mu_0$ — it does not represent the null distribution 3. **One-sample bootstrap test:** shift data so $\bar{x}^* = \theta_0$, resample, compute the t-statistic; the p-value is the fraction of bootstrap statistics as extreme as observed 4. **Bootstrap vs. t-test:** the bootstrap requires only iid sampling and no distributional assumptions; benefits are largest at small $n$ with skewed or heavy-tailed data; both converge for large $n$ 5. **Duality is approximate, not exact:** the bootstrap percentile CI and bootstrap t-test use different pivots, so near CI boundaries with small, skewed samples they can give contradictory decisions — reject by one criterion but not the other ::: ## Looking Ahead **Next class: Two-Sample z and t Tests; Confidence Intervals** - Two-sample z-test for means ($\sigma$ known) - Welch t-test for means ($\sigma$ unknown) - Pooled t-test (equal variance assumption) - Two-sample inference for proportions . . . **Later: Permutation and Bootstrap Tests for Two Samples (C&H Ch. 8)** - Label-permutation tests for two independent groups - One-sample sign-flip permutation test - Bootstrap two-sample test ## References ::: nonincremental - Chihara, L. M. and Hesterberg, T. C. *Mathematical Statistics with Resampling and R* (Wiley). Chapter 8: Bootstrap Hypothesis Testing. - Devore, Berk, and Carlton. *Modern Mathematical Statistics with Applications* (Springer). Section 9.6. - Efron, B. and Hastie, T. (2016). *Computer Age Statistical Inference*. Cambridge University Press. Chapter 15. ::: ## Questions? {.center background-color="#3498db"} Thank you!

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
